body.text: Kazakhstan announced in June 2025 that it would build its first nuclear power plant in partnership with a consortium led by Russia’s Rosatom. Almost immediately afterward, Astana announced that it would build its second with China. As the shape of that project begins to take form, the country’s authorities have set 2035 as the target date for both to be completed.

Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant is planned for a site near the village of Ulken, in Almaty Region on the shore of Lake Balkhash. The second plant will also be near Balkhash. It’s name, Moyynkum, was revealed earlier this year. Meanwhile, Kazakhstan is considering two locations – either in the east or west of the country – for a third nuclear power plant.

This week, Kazakh Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said during a government briefing that “[t]he first Balkhash NPP [nuclear power plant] will be built with the Russian consortium Rosatom, and the second NPP, Moyynkum, is currently being developed with the China National Nuclear Corporation [CNNC].”

In late October, during his annual state of the nation speech, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev iterated his proposal to turn the country into a “big construction site.” This endeavor includes Astana’s nuclear power ambitions. He referred to nuclear power as being of “fundamental importance,” and praised as the “correct decision” the approval of a referendum on the topic in 2024. That referendum took place under heavy government pressure on critics of nuclear power.

Tokayev went on to note that Kazakhstan needs more than just nuclear power plants; it needs to develop a whole host of facilities and human capital. “It is important to engage foreign partners involved in the construction of nuclear power plants, the creation of high-tech production facilities in Kazakhstan, the transfer of nuclear energy expertise, and the training of domestic nuclear specialists,” he said. “Such proposals are being received from Russian and Chinese companies.”

Tokayev then said that it was possible, “perhaps necessary,” to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP in 2027 and also to “sign a comprehensive cooperation agreement with the goal of promptly commencing construction of the Moyynkum NPP.”

In June, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited the Kazakh capital to plant an oak tree in the “Alley of Eternal Friendship between Kazakhstan and Russia,” and oversee the signing of a dozen agreements, including several related to the nuclear power plant project. Among those agreements was one on the provision of a state export loan from Russia to Kazakhstan to finance the project.

While the exact details of Russia’s export loan to Kazakhstan have not been revealed, it was reported that Moscow was furnishing as much as 85 percent of the project’s financing. The Balkhash NPP includes pair of VVER-1200 III+ reactors with a combined capacity of 2.4 GWe. In August 2025 survey work began on the project, the pricetag on which was stated as $14-15 billion at the time. As of June 2026, that figure has grown to around $16.4 billion.
Akkenzhenov, the energy minister, said that the details of the second nuclear power plant project are currently under discussion with China’s CNNC.
“The parameters of the project are currently being discussed, including the terms of the deal and the timeline. We believe that the projects should be completed by 2035,” he said.

That is the timeline Kazakh authorities have cited previously for the Balkhash nuclear power plant – construction starting in 2027 and operations beginning by 2035. For Moyynkum, it seems more of a stretch since there isn’t even a deal settled.

Earlier, when Kazakh authorities were considering offers to lead the consortium for the first plant, CNNC had proposed its HPR-1000. Also known as a Hualong One, the HPR-1000 is a generation III+ pressurized water reactor like Rosatom’s VVER-1200 III+ with a similar electrical output. Presumably that’s what’s on offer. Tengrinews reported in April, when the second plant’s name was revealed, “It is expected that the new NPP will consist of two power units with a capacity of 1,200 megawatts each.”

As for Kazakhstan’s third nuclear power plant, the chairman of the country’s Atomic Energy Agency, lmassadam Satkaliyev, said on November 2 that Astana is considering a medium-capacity plant of 300 to 600 MW – considerably smaller than the Balkhash plant as announced or the presumable design of the Moyynkum plant. The options for location include the city of Kurchatov in eastern Kazakhstan’s Abai Region or somewhere in western Kazakhstan, which encompasses the regions of Aktobe, Atyrau, Mangystau, and West Kazakhstan.
